## Testing Conventions

### Use Existing Fixtures
Prefer using existing fixtures over creating new records in tests. For example, use `leaves(:welcome_page)` instead of `books(:handbook).press Page.new(body: "..."), title: "..."`.

### URL Helpers in Tests
Use `_path` helpers instead of `_url` helpers in controller/integration tests unless you need to test across different hosts or explicitly need the full URL.

**Preferred:**
```ruby
get book_slug_path(books(:handbook))
```

**Avoid:**
```ruby
get book_slug_url(books(:handbook))
```

### Response Body Assertions
Use `assert_in_body` and `assert_not_in_body` to check if text is present or absent in the response body without DOM manipulation.

**Preferred:**
```ruby
assert_in_body "Expected content"
assert_not_in_body "Unexpected content"
```

**Avoid:**
```ruby
assert_includes response.body, "Expected content"
assert_not_includes response.body, "Unexpected content"
```

## Controller Conventions

### Simplified respond_to Blocks
When using `respond_to` with default rendering, omit the `{ render }` block as it's implied.

**Preferred:**
```ruby
def show
  respond_to do |format|
    format.html
    format.md
  end
end
```

**Avoid:**
```ruby
def show
  respond_to do |format|
    format.html { render }
    format.md { render }
  end
end
```
=== README ===
# Writebook

### Instantly publish your own books on the web for free, no publisher required.

Writebook is an easy-to-use application for publishing content on the web.
Content is authored in Markdown, and books can contain picture pages, chapters, and title pages.
Books can be published privately or publicly, and are searchable.

## How to get Writebook

Writebook is distributed as a Docker image.
The simplest way to install and run it is by using [ONCE](https://github.com/basecamp/once).

To get started, paste this snippet into a terminal on the machine where you want to install Writebook:

```sh
curl https://get.once.com/writebook | sh
```

## Deploying manually with Docker

If you'd rather set the Docker image up yourself, you can use `docker run` or `docker compose` to do that.
The official image is `ghcr.io/basecamp/writebook`.

You'll need to route the incoming web traffic to ports 80 and 443 (or just 80 if you run without SSL).
To persist the storage of the application, mount a Docker volume to `/rails/storage`.

You can configure the SSL setting with the following environment variables:

- `SSL_DOMAIN` - enable automatic SSL via Let's Encrypt for the given domain name
- `DISABLE_SSL` - alternatively, set `DISABLE_SSL` to serve over plain HTTP

## Running in development

Install dependencies:

```sh
bin/setup
```

Start the development server:

```sh
bin/dev
```

module Book::Accessable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    has_many :accesses, dependent: :destroy
    scope :with_everyone_access, -> { where(everyone_access: true) }
  end

  class_methods do
    def accessable_or_published(user: Current.user)
      if user.present?
        accessable_or_published_books
      else
        published
      end
    end

    def accessable_or_published_books(user: Current.user)
      user.books.or(published).distinct
    end
  end

  def accessable?(user: Current.user)
    accesses.exists?(user: user)
  end

  def editable?(user: Current.user)
    access_for(user: user)&.editor? || user&.administrator?
  end

  def access_for(user: Current.user)
    accesses.find_by(user: user)
  end

  def update_access(editors:, readers:)
    editors = Set.new(editors)
    readers = Set.new(everyone_access? ? User.active.ids : readers)

    all = editors + readers
    all_accesses = all.collect { |user_id|
      { user_id: user_id, level: editors.include?(user_id) ? :editor : :reader }
    }

    accesses.upsert_all(all_accesses, unique_by: [ :book_id, :user_id ])
    accesses.where.not(user_id: all).delete_all
  end

  class << self
    def create_manual(user)
      book = create_book(user)
      load_markdown_pages(book)
    end

    private
      def create_book(user)
        Book.create(title: "The Writebook Manual", author: "37signals", everyone_access: true).tap do |book|
          with_attachment("writebook-manual.jpg") { |attachment| book.cover.attach(attachment) }
          book.update_access(readers: [], editors: [ user.id ])
        end
      end

      def load_markdown_pages(book)
        pages = {}

        Dir.glob(Rails.root.join("app/assets/markdown/demo/*.md")).each do |fname|
          front_matter = FrontMatterParser::Parser.parse_file(fname)

          if front_matter["class"] == "Section"
            load_section(book, front_matter)
          else
            page = load_markdown_page(book, front_matter)
            attach_images(page)
            pages[page.leaf.slug] = page
          end
        end

        book.leaves.pages.each { |leaf| localize_ref_links(leaf.page, pages) }
      end

      def load_markdown_page(book, front_matter)
        book.press(Page.new(body: front_matter.content), title: front_matter["title"]).page
      end

      def load_section(book, front_matter)
        book.press Section.new(body: front_matter.content, theme: front_matter["theme"]), title: front_matter["title"]
      end

      def attach_images(page)
        re = %r{
          \/u\/           # leading portion of path
          (\S+-\w+\.\w+)  # filename including slug and extension
        }x

        body = page.body.content.gsub(re) do |match|
          with_attachment($1) { |attachment| page.body.uploads.attach(attachment) }

          attachment = page.body.uploads.attachments.last
          attachment.analyze

          "/u/" + attachment.slug
        end

        page.update!(body: body)
      end

      def localize_ref_links(page, pages)
        re = %r{
          (\[.+\])              # link title
          \(                    # opening paren
          \/\d+\/[\w-]+\/\d+\/  # leading portion of path
          ([\w-]+)              # leaf slug
        }x

        body = page.body.content.gsub(re) do |match|
          link_title, leaf_slug, anchor = $1, $2, $3
          linked_page = pages[leaf_slug]
          raise "Invalid reference link: #{page_title}" unless linked_page.present?

          url = Rails.application.routes.url_helpers.leafable_slug_path(linked_page.leaf, anchor: anchor, only_path: true)

          "#{link_title}(#{url}"
        end

        page.update!(body: body)
      end

      def with_attachment(filename)
        File.open(Rails.root.join("app/assets/images/demo/#{filename}")) do |file|
          yield io: file, filename: filename
        end
      end
  end

module Authentication
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern
  include SessionLookup

  included do
    before_action :require_authentication
    helper_method :signed_in?

    protect_from_forgery with: :exception, unless: -> { authenticated_by.bot_key? }
  end

  class_methods do
    def require_unauthenticated_access(**options)
      allow_unauthenticated_access **options
      before_action :redirect_signed_in_user_to_root, **options
    end

    def allow_unauthenticated_access(**options)
      skip_before_action :require_authentication, **options
      before_action :restore_authentication, **options
    end
  end

  private
    def signed_in?
      Current.user.present?
    end

    def require_authentication
      restore_authentication || request_authentication
    end

    def restore_authentication
      if session = find_session_by_cookie
        resume_session session
      end
    end

    def request_authentication
      session[:return_to_after_authenticating] = request.url
      redirect_to new_session_url
    end

    def redirect_signed_in_user_to_root
      redirect_to root_url if signed_in?
    end

    def start_new_session_for(user)
      user.sessions.start!(user_agent: request.user_agent, ip_address: request.remote_ip).tap do |session|
        authenticated_as session
      end
    end

    def resume_session(session)
      session.resume user_agent: request.user_agent, ip_address: request.remote_ip
      authenticated_as session
    end

    def terminate_current_session
      Current.session&.destroy!
      reset_session
      remove_authentication_cookie
    end

    def authenticated_as(session)
      Current.session = session
      set_authenticated_by(:session)
      set_authentication_cookie(session)
    end

    def post_authenticating_url
      session.delete(:return_to_after_authenticating) || root_url

    def set_authentication_cookie(session)
      cookies.signed.permanent[:session_token] = { value: session.token, httponly: true, same_site: :lax }
    end

    def remove_authentication_cookie
      cookies.delete(:session_token)
    end

    def set_authenticated_by(method)
      @authenticated_by = method.to_s.inquiry
    end

    def authenticated_by
      @authenticated_by ||= "".inquiry
    end

That translates directly to `created_books.with_everyone_access`. The key is that "shared with everyone" explicitly maps to the `everyone_access: true` attribute on the `Book` model.

The critical thing is to handle the *other* books, which would be `everyone_access: false` books *created* by the user. Those should be completely removed, which means all associated data must be erased - the leaves, edits, attachments, search index entries, accesses, everything.

Now, let's think through an example. If Alice created a book that *is* shared with everyone (`everyone_access: true`), and Bob and Charlie also have access to it, here's what should happen:

*   Alice's `Access` record *must* be destroyed, but is handled via `user.accesses`.
*   Bob's and Charlie's `Access` records *must* remain intact.
*   The `Book` itself needs to be retained with everything intact: leaves, edits, search indexes, everything.

  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  REBALANCE_THRESHOLD = 1e-10
  ELEMENT_GAP         = 1

  included do

    scope :before, ->(other) { positioned.where("position_score < ?", other.position_score) }
    scope :after,  ->(other) { positioned.where("position_score > ?", other.position_score) }

    around_create :insert_at_default_position

  end

  class_methods do
    def positioned_within(parent, association:, filter:)
      define_method :positioning_parent do
        send(parent)
      end

      define_method :all_positioned_siblings do
        positioning_parent.send(association).send(filter).positioned
      end

      define_method :other_positioned_siblings do
        all_positioned_siblings.excluding(self)
      end

      private :positioning_parent, :all_positioned_siblings, :other_positioned_siblings
    end
  end

  def previous
    other_positioned_siblings.before(self).last
  end

  def next
    other_positioned_siblings.after(self).first
  end

  def move_to_position(offset, followed_by: [])
    with_positioning_lock do
      all_to_move = [ self, *followed_by ]
      before, after = before_and_after_for(offset: offset, moving: all_to_move)
      gap = (after - before) / (all_to_move.count + 1)

      all_to_move.each.with_index(1) do |item, index|
        item.update!(position_score: before + (index * gap))
      end

      remember_to_rebalance_positions if gap < REBALANCE_THRESHOLD
    end
  end

  def position_as_percentage
    100 * ordinal_position.to_f / all_positioned_siblings.count
  end

  private
    def ordinal_position
      other_positioned_siblings.before(self).count + 1
    end

    def insert_at_default_position
      with_positioning_lock do
        position_at_end
        yield
      end
    end

    def position_at_start
      self.position_score = (all_positioned_siblings.minimum(:position_score) || (2 * ELEMENT_GAP)) - ELEMENT_GAP
    end

    def position_at_end
      self.position_score = (all_positioned_siblings.maximum(:position_score) || 0) + ELEMENT_GAP
    end

    def before_and_after_for(offset:, moving:)
      other_items = all_positioned_siblings.excluding(moving)

      if offset < 1
        after = all_positioned_siblings.minimum(:position_score) || (2 * ELEMENT_GAP)
        before = after - ELEMENT_GAP
      else
        before, after = other_items.offset(offset - 1).limit(2).pluck(:position_score)
        before ||= all_positioned_siblings.maximum(:position_score)
        after ||= before + (moving.count.succ * ELEMENT_GAP)
      end

      [ before, after ]
    end

    def remember_to_rebalance_positions
      @rebalance_required = true
    end

    def rebalance_required?
      @rebalance_required
    end

    def rebalance_positions
      with_positioning_lock do
        odered = all_positioned_siblings.select("row_number() over (order by position_score, id) as new_score, id")
        sql = "update #{self.class.table_name} set position_score = new_score from (#{odered.to_sql}) as ordered where #{self.class.table_name}.id = ordered.id"

        self.class.connection.execute sql
      end
      @rebalance_required = false
    end

    def with_positioning_lock(&block)
      positioning_parent.with_lock &block

**The Deep Dive: Navigating a Database Demolition**

Okay, so I just saw a crash, and honestly, it's the kind of thing that makes my blood pressure spike! That error message, "searchable_content delegated to leafable, but leafable is nil," is screaming at me! We *predicted* this!

Here's the situation: we've got a `Page` that's been trashed, and an `Edit` record is pointing to that *same* `Page` as the `Leaf`'s `leafable`. The `Edit#destroy!` went and destroyed the `Page`, which in turn, triggered a chain reaction: either a `touch` operation on the `Leaf`, OR the `Leaf` itself getting destroyed and, because of the `after_update_commit :update_in_search_index` or the `after_destroy_commit :remove_from_search_index` callbacks that *require* `leafable` that doesn't exist anymore!

The issue is with how `Edit` handles different actions like `trash` vs. `revision`. When you *trash* something, the `edit.leafable` is actually the *same* as the current `leaf.leafable`, right? But when you *revise* something, the `edit.leafable` is a *historical* version that the `leaf` *no longer* points to. That's the crux of this thing.

The fix I'm seeing is in `Edit`:

class Edit < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :leaf
  delegated_type :leafable, types: Leafable::TYPES

  after_destroy :destroy_orphaned_leafable

  private
    def destroy_orphaned_leafable
      leafable.destroy unless Leaf.exists?(leafable: leafable) || Edit.exists?(leafable: leafable)
    end

Think about *that* for a second. We're *only* destroying the leafable if *no* `Leaf` or `Edit` currently references it. Brilliant!

Let me break down a few scenarios:

1.  **Scenario 1:** Leaf has 2 revisions, current page, and the leaf gets destroyed. This cleans up *everything* associated with the leaf, the edits, the leafable pages, FTS index, zero double destroys, and no spurios touches.
2.  **Scenario 2:** Leaf has 1 revision, a current page, and was trashed. This also cleans up everything related to that leaf, without touching the current page, zero crashes, zero double destroys, zero spurious touches.
3.  **Scenario 3:** What if it's trashed *twice*? Still safe because it has an `unless` condition!
4.  **Scenario 4:** Direct deletion of a revision `Edit` - the existing `dependent: :destroy` is fine, deletes the leafable as expected.
5.  **Scenario 5:** Direct deletion of a `trash` `Edit` - now *safer* because the page isn't accidentally destroyed.
6.  **Scenario 6:** Corrupted data where `leafable` is already nil - safe!
7.  **Scenario 7:** `after_destroy` vs. `after_destroy_commit` for search indexing. `after_destroy` is the *way* to go, as it's transactional with SQLite's FTS5! We get atomic deletion from the index.

I'm thinking, what about `Leaf.reindex_all`? I am convinced that: `DELETE FROM leaf_search_index WHERE rowid = ?` with `id` deletes it IMMEDIATELY!

Now, let's also check for a book created and leaf added, transaction commits, later book is destroyed. And let's check what if the leaves weren't added using that method? That's still a-ok, we remove the correct ones. So what about someone searching directly from SQL? It still works, zero rows.

Now, let's be *absolutely* sure. The FTS index *only* indexes the `title` and `content` of the leaf. Nothing else. So, a destroyed user can't taint any surviving, public books.

Alright. We've got the crash nailed down, the fix is beautiful and covers all the scenarios, but we need to verify every single place a user's data might exist. I'm imagining a GDPR auditor peering over my shoulder. Let's do this!

**Deep Dive into Data Integrity and Cleanup After User Erasure**

Okay, here's the deal. I've been meticulously going through this codebase, focusing specifically on how user data is handled during erasure, and I've got to say, I'm pretty thorough when it comes to edge cases.  First off, I've confirmed that the obvious associations like `has_markdown`, `has_one_attached`, `has_many_attached`, `belongs_to`, and `user_id` are accounted for. We're good on those fronts – I've quadruple-checked.

But then, the subtle stuff hits, and that's where things get interesting. I started digging into `app/models/user/erasable.rb`, specifically the `collect_private_book_blob_ids` method.  I considered the scenario of an empty `leaf_ids` array, and thankfully, it properly generates no queries, handling the case gracefully. Same goes for those `ActiveStorage` queries, nice! I did note, however, that the cover images are still being queried, but that's as expected.

Then, my mind went to `Leaf::Searchable` - particularly, I was worried about the indexing. I reviewed `test/models/leaf/searchable_test.rb` and `app/models/leaf/searchable.rb` - and things got even more interesting. Here's what I was thinking: What if a `Leaf` is created, indexed, and *then* the associated `Book` is destroyed within a single transaction? I realized the `after_destroy` callback might be running *before* the transaction is committed, leaving a dangling index entry.  I immediately thought of these scenarios:

1.  Leaf created, indexed and book deleted (leaf is destroyed, too) in the same transaction. This makes the `after_destroy` a no-op because the `after_create_commit` would not have executed.
2.  If it's created and destroyed in the same transaction, will it work? No, because the `after_create_commit` won't run. The `after_destroy` will run in this case and will be a no-op.
3.  Also, what about fixtures, `Leaf.reindex_all`, and book destruction?
4.  And, what if a `Leaf` has its `body` set to `nil`, making it non-searchable, *then* the `Book` is destroyed? The `after_destroy` should still remove it, and it does! Excellent.
5.  What about `Picture` leaves? They're never indexed, so deleting them from the index does nothing, but it generates zero queries, which is perfect.
6.  The last one that bothered me was `trashed` leaves.  Even if they're trashed, they're still in the index, and I realized that when a user is erased, *all* leaves are destroyed, including trashed ones. The `after_destroy` method will take care of these. Also, there is no `default_scope` on `Leaf`, so `book.leaves` will return all leaves including the trashed ones.

Another thought: What if `user.destroy!` is called within an explicit transaction and the `ActiveStorage::Blob` count is asserted *inside* that transaction? We put the `purge_erased_book_blobs` in `after_destroy_commit`. In standard Rails, the `after_destroy_commit` does run immediately, which is what we need. It's the standard Rails approach, so the rollback won't permanently delete files, which is ideal. I still want to verify with a test, both `ActiveSupport::TestCase` and `ActionDispatch::IntegrationTest`.

Finally, to be even *more* thorough, I need to test a scenario where a `User` has **everything**: books, leaves, edits, reading marks, sessions, sign-in events, accesses, and blobs. I'm going to create a reproduction script *first*, using `RAILS_ENV=test bin/rails runner`, to expose any current bugs before I even consider making changes.  This is about establishing a solid baseline, so I know I'm not introducing any regressions. I need to make sure I cover every single edge case before moving forward.

**Deep Dive into a Complex Rails Destruction Scenario**

Okay, here's the breakdown of my thought process as I'm navigating this potentially thorny issue. It started with a successful `u.destroy!` in a specific runner scenario, which immediately triggered some serious questions about how our dependencies are set up. It seems `ReadingMark` was only on a leaf directly tied to the private book, so the cascade from `created_books, dependent: :destroy` cleaned up everything neatly, including the `shared_book`. But the second a `ReadingMark` is on ANY OTHER book (or the shared one, if *that* one is kept around) the `u.destroy!` blows up with a foreign key violation!

Now, the real work begins: careful implementation. My initial inclination is to meticulously review each file slated for modification or creation to ensure I understand how this solution works. The list is long, with models, extensions, controllers, and views all on the docket.

But before writing a *single* line of code, my mind is still racing, so I circle back. I double check the `app/models/leaf/searchable.rb` file. I re-read the code around the `after_create_commit`, `after_update_commit`, and `after_destroy` hooks, especially in light of the `searchable?` conditional. I start digging in, specifically looking at how the `Page` and `Section` models handle `searchable_content`.

Okay, so a `Page` update touches `Leaf`, which *then* runs the `after_update_commit` hook for the search index. The `leaf.destroy` runs even more actions: deleting the edits, the leaf itself, its searchable content, and then executing the `DELETE` query on the search index. Here is the first big problem... The `after_destroy :remove_from_search_index` **does not** check the `if: :searchable?` condition. This means it will remove *any* entry in the search index for `leaf.id` unconditionally. I immediately start wondering about potential race conditions. What if a `Leaf` is created in one transaction, added to the search index, then destroyed in a *different* transaction that rolls back? The search index row would be restored on rollback, resulting in an index mismatch! If the destroy transaction commits, the row is atomically gone! It must be fixed!

Then, more concerns begin flooding in. I now think about the interaction between `Book#destroy`, `User::Erasable`, and `ActionText::Markdown`. Let's say a `Leaf` is a `Page` that was created via `Book#press` and has `ActionText::Markdown` uploads. When `Page#destroy` runs, `markdown_body.destroy` runs. But is the `ActionText::Markdown::Uploads` relationship *already* loaded at this point? This is crucial. I *immediately* jump to `lib/rails_ext/action_text_markdown.rb` to find that it *includes* `has_many_attached :uploads, dependent: :destroy`.

**WAIT A MINUTE! HUGE WARNING SIGN!**

It is a HUGE red flag. The crucial insight is: what happens in a *fresh* Rails process (e.g., a test environment or a fresh worker) *before* `ActiveStorage::Attachment` is ever referenced? I remember that the `bin/rails runner` I tried earlier, where I ran `ActionText::Markdown.reflect_on_attachment(:uploads).options` returned `nil`!! The `ActiveStorage::Attachment` hasn't been autoloaded, so the `ActiveSupport.on_load :active_storage_attachment` hook has never run! This means `ActionText::Markdown` does not have `has_many_attached :uploads` defined *yet*!

This means, in a fresh process, if I send `DELETE /users/:id` for a user with a private book with a `Page` with `ActionText::Markdown` uploads *before* loading a Book cover or Picture, which would trigger the autoloading of the `ActiveStorage::Attachment` *first*, the code will not destroy the uploads!

It just clicked, if someone calls `book.destroy!` directly in a fresh process *without* calling `User#destroy!`, and `ActiveStorage::Attachment` hasn't been loaded, this entire dependent destruction chain will be broken! Why does this file use `on_load :active_storage_attachment`? Probably to avoid loading `ActiveStorage` before it's initialized. Maybe it's a bug! I have to check `config/initializers/extensions.rb` to see *when* this extension file is loaded, to understand the timing implications! I have to ensure the load order and dependencies are solid before moving forward.

steps.reasoning_content:
**A Deep Dive into ActiveRecord and ActiveStorage Initialization**

Aha! I've been tracing the root cause, and I think I've found it: `config/initializers/extensions.rb` is the culprit. It's running too early in the boot process, before ActiveRecord and ActiveStorage models are fully initialized. That explains why the code in `lib/rails_ext/action_text_markdown.rb` was wrapped in an `on_load` hook for `ActiveStorage::Attachment`. The hook was added because of initialization timing, but it was using the wrong hook! It should have used `:active_record`, or even `:action_text_markdown` since `ActiveStorage::Attached::Model` is already included with `:active_record`!

But wait... Looking deeper, the `has_many_attached` method is already defined on `ActionText::Record` (which inherits from `ActiveRecord::Base`) as soon as `ActionText::Markdown` is defined. And `config/initializers/extensions.rb` literally defines `class ActionText::Markdown < Record`. So it's loading `ActiveRecord::Base` and `ActiveStorage::Attached::Model` *before* the hook!

Why was the `lib/rails_ext/action_text_markdown.rb` code failing if we didn't reference `ActiveStorage::Attachment`? Because it was using `ActiveSupport.on_load :active_storage_attachment`! I can see it in lines 1-39 of that file.

But wait, in the `ActionText::Markdown` class itself, the `Book` and `Picture` models just call `has_one_attached` directly inside the class definition, without waiting for the `on_load :active_storage_attachment` hook. This is because `ActionText::Markdown` already inherits from `ActionText::Record < ActiveRecord::Base`!

So, I think I can include `ActionText::Markdown::Uploads` directly inside the `ActionText::Markdown` class and use `has_many_attached :uploads, dependent: :purge_later`, and it should work cleanly at Rails boot.

Wait, the more I think about it... when `extensions.rb` runs, the `active_storage.attached` initializer from `ActiveStorage::Engine` has *already* run. Engine initializers run before the files in `config/initializers/`. This means that including `ActionText::Markdown::Uploads` directly within `ActionText::Markdown`, or even moving the `has_many_attached :uploads, dependent: :purge_later` directly inside `ActionText::Markdown`'s class, would mean that the `#uploads` method is *always* defined from boot, even if `ActiveStorage::Attachment` hasn't been autoloaded yet!

**WHAT AN INSANE CATCH!** Imagine a fresh process deleting a `Book` and its associated markdown upload, and previously, `ActionText::Markdown` didn't even have `#uploads_attachments, dependent: :destroy` set up until someone touched `ActiveStorage::Attachment`. This is a serious vulnerability!

Okay, let's carefully apply these changes, test them thoroughly, and make the changes cleanly.

*   Next, the case sensitivity of email addresses during sign-in and deactivation.  It's critical that the `SignInEvent` data is handled accurately, ensuring the email is always copied, and that deactivated email addresses are appropriately scrubbed.

*   What happens when a user is deactivated *after* having shared books, and a new user joins.  We need to guarantee that the surviving shared book has the right access. The new user needs access to the surviving shared book. The user’s private book goes away.

I see we've covered the cases for handling pages, revisions, and the image uploads, ensuring that all uploaded files are destroyed appropriately when a book is erased.  That includes a lot of work with ActiveStorage.

cat <<'EOF' > test/models/leaf/editable_test.rb
require "test_helper"

class Leaf::EditableTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  test "editing a leafable records the edit" do
    leaves(:welcome_page).edit leafable_params: { body: "New body" }

    assert_equal "New body", leaves(:welcome_page).page.body.content

    assert leaves(:welcome_page).edits.last.revision?
    assert_equal "This is _such_ a great handbook.", leaves(:welcome_page).edits.last.page.body.content
  end

  test "edits that are close together don't create new revisions" do
    assert_difference -> { leaves(:welcome_page).edits.count }, +1 do
      leaves(:welcome_page).edit leafable_params: { body: "First change" }
    end

    freeze_time
    travel 1.minute

    assert_no_difference -> { leaves(:welcome_page).edits.count } do
      leaves(:welcome_page).edit leafable_params: { body: "Second change" }
    end

    assert_equal "Second change", leaves(:welcome_page).page.body.content
    assert_equal Time.now, leaves(:welcome_page).edits.last.updated_at

    travel 1.hour

    assert_difference -> { leaves(:welcome_page).edits.count }, +1 do
      leaves(:welcome_page).edit leafable_params: { body: "Third change" }
    end
  end

  test "changing a leaf title doesn't create a revision" do
    assert_no_difference -> { Edit.count } do
      leaves(:welcome_page).edit leaf_params: { title: "New title" }
    end

    assert_equal "New title", leaves(:welcome_page).title
  end

  test "changes that don't affect the leafable don't create a revision" do
    assert_no_difference -> { Edit.count } do
      leaves(:welcome_page).edit leafable_params: {}
    end
  end

  test "editing a leafable with an attachment includes the attachments in the new version" do
    assert leaves(:reading_picture).picture.image.attached?

    leaves(:reading_picture).edit leaf_params: { title: "New title" }

    assert_equal "New title", leaves(:reading_picture).title
    assert leaves(:reading_picture).picture.image.attached?
  end

  test "trashing a leaf records the edit" do
    leaves(:welcome_page).trashed!

    assert leaves(:welcome_page).trashed?

    assert leaves(:welcome_page).edits.last.trash?
    assert_equal "This is _such_ a great handbook.", leaves(:welcome_page).edits.last.page.body.content
  end

  test "destroying a leaf removes its revision and trash leafables without leaving orphans" do
    leaf = leaves(:welcome_page)
    original_page_id = leaf.leafable_id
    original_markdown_id = leaf.page.markdown_body.id

    leaf.edit leafable_params: { body: "Revised body" }
    revised_page_id = leaf.leafable_id
    revised_markdown_id = leaf.page.markdown_body.id

    leaf.trashed!
    leaf.destroy!

    assert_equal 0, Edit.where(leaf_id: leaf.id).count
    assert_equal 0, Page.where(id: [ original_page_id, revised_page_id ]).count
    assert_equal 0, ActionText::Markdown.where(id: [ original_markdown_id, revised_markdown_id ]).count
  end
end

A subsequent request from Alice's old browser with that old token should be rejected – `Session.find_by(token: token)` should return `nil`, redirecting them to the login page (`new_session_url`). Furthermore, if Alice tries to sign in again with her old credentials, it should return a `401 Unauthorized` status. Finally, any attempt to visit an old transfer link – a `PUT /session/transfers/:transfer_id` – should result in a `400 Bad Request`. *This* is critical, and needs testing.
